slides.1.title: The Four Main Soils and Their Regions
slides.1.items.0.label: Schist (Xisto)
slides.1.items.0.desc: The main soil of the Douro Valley. It retains heat well, and roots can penetrate up to 20 metres in search of water, giving mineral and smoky notes
slides.1.items.1.label: Granite (Granito)
slides.1.items.1.desc: Minho, Dão and Trás-os-Montes. Well drained, giving wines lively, fresh minerality and a fine texture
slides.1.items.2.label: Clay-limestone
slides.1.items.2.desc: Bairrada and parts of Lisboa. Heavy and water-retentive, giving Baga its firm acidity and tannins
slides.1.items.3.label: Sand (Areia)
slides.1.items.3.desc: Colares coastal area. The sand dunes protect vines from phylloxera, making them the last refuge of the ancient Ramisco variety
slides.2.title: Douro's Schist: The Foundation of Port
slides.2.html:
The most important soil in the Douro Valley is schist (Xisto) — a dark grey-black, thinly layered metamorphic rock.

🌱 Why Is Schist So Important to the Douro?

  • Excellent heat retention: absorbs the sun's heat by day and releases it slowly at night, extending the ripening period
  • Vertical fissures: roots can penetrate 10–20 metres deep in search of groundwater
  • Poor soil: low yields but high concentration, giving Port and Douro reds great depth of fruit
  • Minerality: brings distinctive graphite, mineral and spice complexity

It is precisely these harsh soil conditions that create world-class wines on the Douro's steep terraces.
slides.3.question: What is the main soil type of the Douro Valley?
slides.3.explanation: Schist (Xisto) is the main soil of the Douro Valley. It retains heat well and its vertical fissures let roots go deep, an important foundation of Port quality.
